pioneer-square.name: Pioneer Square & Smith Tower
pioneer-square.blurb: Seattle's 1890s birthplace: the cast-iron 1909 pergola, the Tlingit-style totem pole, red-brick Romanesque blocks, the Underground and the white terracotta Smith Tower (1914).

spawn.note: 1st Ave S sidewalk south of the pergola, looking north at pergola + Pioneer Building + totem pole.

extent.description: Pioneer Place (triangular plaza at 1st Ave & Yesler Way): pergola, totem pole, Chief Seattle bust; Pioneer Building; Yesler Way east to Smith Tower at 2nd Ave; Occidental Ave S pedestrian mall south to Occidental Square (totems, firefighters memorial); Underground Tour entrance; 1st Ave historic façades.
extent.edges: Columbia St (north), 2nd Ave (east), S Main St (south), Alaskan Way/Western Ave hill (west).
extent.vertical: Gentle slope up east along Yesler Way toward 2nd Ave (≈ +8 m).

structures.name: Pioneer Square Pergola (1909, Julian F. Everett; rebuilt 2002)
structures.form: Victorian triangular cast-iron and glass shelter: slender fluted iron columns, ornate brackets and cresting, glass roof panes, hanging lantern lights; bollards and posts protect it after truck strikes (2001 destroyed, 2008/2012 stopped); the closed underground restroom below.
structures.details: Long low triangular canopy with arched gable ends and ornate cresting; posts carry clusters of white globe lamps; low iron railing with planters around; plaza shaded by large London plane trees; trolleybus overhead wires on 1st Ave/Yesler.

structures.name: Pioneer Square totem pole (replica 1938–40, carved by Charles Brown et al.)
structures.form: Tall carved red-cedar Tlingit-style pole replicating one taken from a Tlingit village in Alaska in 1899; stacked figures (raven at top), carved and painted in black, red, blue-green on natural grey-brown cedar.
structures.cultural_note: Treat respectfully: interpretive plaque about the 1899 theft and the replica; no climbing, no jokes in dialogue.

plaques.title: The pergola
plaques.text: Built in 1909 to shelter cable-car passengers, the pergola was destroyed by a truck in 2001 and rebuilt in 2002 using 99% original material.

plaques.title: Underground Seattle
plaques.text: After the Great Fire of June 6, 1889, streets were raised by up to a storey, leaving old sidewalks and storefronts below — the Seattle Underground.

plaques.title: Purple glass
plaques.text: The glass prisms in the sidewalks are vault lights that once lit the buried sidewalks; the clear glass later turned amethyst.

plaques.title: Smith Tower
plaques.text: Completed in 1914 at 462 ft, Smith Tower was the tallest building on the West Coast until the Space Needle in 1962.

plaques.title: The totem pole
plaques.text: The original pole was taken from a Tlingit village in Alaska in 1899; today's pole is a replica carved in 1938–40.

interaction.primary: Underground descent: a short scripted walk below the sidewalk among old storefronts, looking up at the purple vault lights from beneath.
secondary: Ride the Smith Tower brass elevator to the 35th-floor observatory deck (view to the Needle and stadiums)

lines.text: Underground Tour group, gather by the pergola, please!
After the Great Fire of 1889 they raised the streets — the old sidewalks are right under your feet.
See the purple glass squares? Skylights for the underground sidewalks; the glass turned amethyst over time.
This pergola was built in 1909, flattened by a truck in 2001, and rebuilt with almost all original iron.
The totem pole is a replica — the original was taken from a Tlingit village in 1899.
Smith Tower, 1914 — the tallest building on the West Coast until the Space Needle.
Elevator operators still run the brass Otis cars up the Smith Tower.
First Thursday art walk tonight — galleries stay open late.
Game day. Everything's going to be blue and green.
A whole city under the city!
Stand under the pergola — classic shot.
The buildings here are so old!
Let's go up Smith Tower.
Red brick is lovely.
Romanesque brick, 1892 — impressive.
There's a tunnel under the street?
The tour starts in five minutes.

dialogueGeneral.usage: Pedestrian set for the Seattle and Bellevue driving districts and as filler in every spot. ctx: greeting|bumped|photographed|idle|spot|rain|honked_at|near_miss; non-English lines carry orig+lang with English text.

tone.note: "Seattle Freeze": locals are described as "very polite but not particularly friendly" to strangers — keep local NPC lines courteous, brief, low-key; few unprompted chats.
Washington ranked 48th of 50 states for extraversion (2008 study cited by Wikipedia) — locals default to nods, "sorry", "you're good".

Honking is rare and seen as rude: ~3 in 4 Northwest drivers said they rarely or never honk (PEMCO 2017); attitudes softened by 2021 (65% say honking at least somewhat appropriate). NPC reaction to player honking near spots: surprised/disapproving, not aggressive.
Coffee culture: Seattle drinks more coffee than any other US city; espresso small talk is a safe icebreaker.
Rain talk is universal small talk; locals rarely use umbrellas (hoods/rain shells) — common local self-image, unsourced folklore: keep light.

Visitors: Canada was 73% of Seattle's 2.4 M international visitors in 2024; then China, India, UK, South Korea, Germany, Japan, Australia, France, Taiwan — languages used: English, French (Québec), Mandarin, Hindi, Korean, German, Japanese, Spanish (domestic + Latin America).
Indigenous art (totems, Salish Welcome): staff/guides speak respectfully; no jokes about sacred objects.
Guardrails: no stereotypes, accents written phonetically, slurs, politics or alcohol jokes about any group; tourists are curious and happy, locals helpful-but-reserved.
